# Exercise 2.2 — Correlation and missingness {#sec-correlation-missing}

This is an example of the great amount of resources available in open-source programming languages, where new packages are developed and made available constantly. As key insight, explore, probably what you need is already out there for you to use!

:::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

### Correlation

For you to see the breadth of possibilities out there, here is an example of different ways in which to describe and learn about the correlation matrix of your dataset.

```{r, message=FALSE}


# Install required libraries (if not already installed)

#install.packages(c("ggplot2", "corrplot", "ggcorrplot", 
#"PerformanceAnalytics", "GGally", "psych", "corrr"))

# Load necessary libraries
library(ggplot2)
library(corrplot)
library(ggcorrplot)
library(PerformanceAnalytics)
library(GGally)
library(psych)
library(corrr)
```

To assess the association between two variables, you can produce a scatter plot like below:

```{r}
set.seed(123)
x <- rnorm(100)
y <- x + rnorm(100, sd = 0.5)

ggplot(data = data.frame(x, y), aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Correlation Plot with ggplot2",
       x = "X values", y = "Y values") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Now we are going to produce the correlation matrix, where in a go, you get insight of all the association happening in your dataset.For this we are going to use the mtcars data (A built-in dataset that contains measurements on 11 different attributes for 32 different cars). More specifically, the chosen variables are:

-   mpg (Miles per Gallon): Represents the fuel efficiency of the car. Higher values, better efficiency.

-   disp (Displacement): Represents the engine displacement, which is the total volume of all the cylinders in the engine.

-   hp (Horsepower): Represents the power output of the car's engine.

-   wt (Weight): Represents the weight of the car.

```{r}
data <- mtcars[, c("mpg", "disp", "hp", "wt")]
```

Can you calculate the correlation between them? Try out at least a pair of functions/packages. Remember there are different ways in which to calculate correlation <https://www.sthda.com/english/wiki/correlation-test-between-two-variables-in-r> and you can specify the type in your code `cor(x, y, method = c("pearson", "kendall", "spearman"))`

```{r}

```

Now that you know what to expect, lets proceed with the correlation matrices (same thing as above, but all in a go!):

#### -----corrplot Correlation Matrix -----

```{r}
cor_matrix <- cor(data)
corrplot(cor_matrix, method = "circle", type = "upper", 
         title = "Correlation Matrix", addCoef.col = "black")
```

#### -----corrplot Correlation Matrix -----

```{r}
ggcorrplot(cor_matrix, 
           method = "square", 
           type = "lower", 
           lab = TRUE, 
           title = "mtcars", 
           lab_size = 3) +
  theme_minimal()
```

#### -----PerformanceAnalytics Pairwise Correlation Plot -----

```{r}
chart.Correlation(data, histogram = TRUE, pch = 19)
```

###-----GGally Pairwise Correlation Plot -----

```{r}
ggpairs(data, 
        title = "Pairwise Correlation Plot with GGally",
        lower = list(continuous = wrap("smooth", method = "lm")),
        upper = list(continuous = wrap("cor", size = 3)))
```

###----- psych Enhanced Pairwise Correlation Plot -----

```{r}
pairs.panels(data, 
             method = "pearson", 
             hist.col = "lightblue", 
             density = TRUE, 
             ellipses = TRUE)
```

###----- Base R Heatmap -----

```{r}
# ----- 8. Base R Heatmap -----
heatmap(cor_matrix, symm = TRUE, 
        main = "Correlation Heatmap", 
        col = colorRampPalette(c("red", "white", "blue"))(20))
```

```{r}
# ----- 10. corrr Tidy Correlation -----
cor_matrix_tidy <- correlate(data)
cor_matrix_tidy %>% 
  fashion() %>% 
  print()

# Network-style correlation plot
cor_matrix_tidy %>% 
  network_plot(min_cor = 0.3)

```

What are your insights? Do they make sense? Remember:

-   mpg (Miles per Gallon): Represents the fuel efficiency of the car. Higher values, better efficiency.

-   disp (Displacement): Represents the engine displacement, which is the total volume of all the cylinders in the engine.

-   hp (Horsepower): Represents the power output of the car's engine.

-   wt (Weight): Represents the weight of the car.

### What a correlation does with values that are not real

`mtcars` is clean. Clinical files are not, and the usual way they are not clean
is that somebody recorded an absent measurement as a number. Before trusting any
of the matrices above, look at `data/diabetes.csv`: 768 adults, eight
measurements and an outcome.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(readr)
library(dplyr)

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")

diabetes |>
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), ~ sum(.x == 0))) |>
  t()
```

A plasma glucose of zero is not a low reading, and a body mass index of zero is
not a thin patient. Both are impossible, so the zero is standing in for "not
measured". Replace the impossible ones with `NA` and compare the two matrices:

```{r}
cols <- c("glucose", "pressure", "triceps", "insulin", "mass")

dia_na <- diabetes |>
  mutate(across(all_of(cols), ~ na_if(.x, 0)))

round(cor(diabetes[cols]), 2)
round(cor(dia_na[cols], use = "pairwise.complete.obs"), 2)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
### The result that should bother you
The strongest association in the raw matrix is mostly an artefact of the zeros,
and one of the real associations was hidden by them. Both directions, in the
same table.

1. **`insulin` with `triceps` falls from about 0.47 to about 0.17** once the
   zeros are treated as missing. Every one of the 251 rows with a zero skin-fold
   also has a zero insulin, so a quarter of the file sits exactly at the origin
   of that scatter plot. Points at the origin, far below the real values, pull a
   regression line through themselves. The association was between the two
   recording failures, not between the two hormonal quantities.
2. **`triceps` with `mass` rises from about 0.38 to about 0.61.** Skin-fold
   thickness and body mass index measure overlapping things and should agree;
   the zeros were diluting that agreement towards the middle.
3. So the zeros did not add noise. Noise attenuates everything. They *moved*
   correlations, up for pairs that share a missingness pattern and down for
   pairs that do not — and nothing in the output marks which is which.
:::

### Missing pipelines

As with the correlation matrices before, there are really good packages to help you understand the missingness structure of your data. This is my recommendation:

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

#Remember, if you do not have these packages installed, install them first with (install.packages())

library(naniar)
library(finalfit)
library(ggplot2)
library(mice)
```

Here I will be using the `airquality` dataset (available as default in all R) but can rerun using your own dataset in a future.

```{r}
summary(airquality)
```

We can already see with a simple summary, the ammount of missings we have per column. But what is their underlying structure?

```{r}
YourDataset <- airquality
```

#### Plot 1

```{r}
ll <- data.frame(is.na(YourDataset))
```

Open up this ll object. What are you seeing here? `is.na()` detects all values coded as `NA` and gives a logical output, `TRUE` if truly a missing value and `FALSE` if not

```{r}
#| eval: false
View(ll)
```

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
cols <- sapply(ll, is.logical)
ll[, cols] <- lapply(ll[, cols], as.numeric)

Miss1 <- UpSetR::upset(ll,
                       nsets = 20, number.angles = 10, point.size = 3.5, line.size = 2,
                       mainbar.y.label = "Missing Values", sets.x.label = "Total Number Missing Values",
                       text.scale = c(2.3, 2.3, 2, 2, 2, 1.75), order.by = "freq", sets.bar.color = "red3"
)


Miss1
```

Here we can see common patterns! If missing values were to happen at the same time in different variables, we would see it clearly. Lets store this figure into our own directories so we can then use it for our final research output!

```{r}
#| eval: false
pdf("MissingVal1.pdf", 10, 20)
print(Miss1)
dev.off()
```

#### Plot 2

```{r}
print(vis_miss(YourDataset, warn_large_data = FALSE) + 
        theme(axis.text.x =  element_text(angle = 90)))


# uncomment to have your pdf created
#pdf("Missing2.pdf", 20, 10)
#print(vis_miss(YourDataset, warn_large_data = FALSE) + 
#        theme(axis.text.x =  element_text(angle = 90)))
#dev.off()
```

Very clear outline of missingness in the whole dataset. But be careful in big datasets!

#### Plot 3

```{r}

missing_pattern(YourDataset)

# uncomment to have your pdf created

#pdf("PlotMissing3.pdf", 4,11)
#
#print(missing_pattern(YourDataset))
#
#dev.off()
#


```

Final, very clear overview of patterns per variable. Spend a moment trying to understand these values. This function works great with big datasets too, although sometimes it gets a bit busy with lots of numbers.


Open up your three newly created pdfs! (remember to uncomment the pdf() lines)


## Python

The same two ideas, without the commentary. `mtcars` and `airquality` are built
into R; in Python the equivalents come from the data folder you downloaded.

```{python}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
heart = pd.read_csv("data/longisland_heart.csv")
```

### Correlation

`pandas` computes the matrix; `seaborn` draws it. These two are the equivalent
of `corrplot` and `ggcorrplot`.

```{python}
cols = ["glucose", "pressure", "triceps", "insulin", "mass"]
cor = diabetes[cols].corr()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4.5))
sns.heatmap(cor, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1, ax=ax)
plt.show()
```

`pairplot` is the equivalent of `ggpairs()` and `pairs.panels()`:

```{python}
sns.pairplot(diabetes[["glucose", "insulin", "mass"]],
             plot_kws=dict(alpha=0.3, s=12), height=1.9)
plt.show()
```

And the same comparison as above — the matrix before and after the impossible
zeros become missing. `.corr()` drops missing pairs by default, which is what
`use = "pairwise.complete.obs"` does in R.

```{python}
dia_na = diabetes.copy()
dia_na[cols] = dia_na[cols].replace(0, np.nan)

print(diabetes[cols].corr().round(2))
print(dia_na[cols].corr().round(2))
```

### Missingness

Counts per column, then the whole file as an image — the equivalent of
`vis_miss()`:

```{python}
print(heart.isna().sum())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.5))
ax.imshow(heart.isna().T, aspect="auto", interpolation="nearest",
          cmap="viridis")
ax.set_yticks(range(heart.shape[1]))
ax.set_yticklabels(heart.columns, fontsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("Patient (row order)")
ax.set_title("Missing values (yellow)")
plt.show()
```

Which columns go missing *together* — the question the UpSet plot answers:

```{python}
pattern = (heart.isna()
           .groupby(list(heart.columns[heart.isna().any()]))
           .size()
           .sort_values(ascending=False)
           .head(8))
print(pattern)
```
